subjects.name: Mercury
clues: A year on this world lasts just 88 Earth days.
It has almost no atmosphere, so its temperatures swing wildly between day and night.
Its cratered grey surface looks a lot like our own Moon.
It is the smallest planet in the solar system.
The planet closest to the Sun.

links.name: Sun
links.rel: is the closest planet to the

subjects.fact: Despite being closest to the Sun, it is not the hottest planet; Venus is.

subjects.name: Venus
clues: It spins backwards compared with most planets, so the Sun rises in the west there.
A day on it is longer than its year.
Thick clouds of sulphuric acid hide its surface from view.
It is the hottest planet, even hotter than Mercury.
Second planet from the Sun, often seen as the bright morning or evening star.

links.name: Sun
links.rel: is the second planet from the

links.name: Earth
links.rel: is often called the twin of

subjects.fact: It is named after the Roman goddess of love and beauty.

subjects.name: Earth
clues: It is the densest planet in the solar system.
About 71 percent of its surface is covered by water.
It has just one large natural satellite.
It is the third planet from the Sun.
The only planet known to support life: our home world.
subjects.fact: It is the only planet in the solar system not named after a god.

subjects.name: Mars
clues: It has the tallest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons.
Its two small moons are named Phobos and Deimos.
Rovers such as Curiosity and Perseverance have explored its surface.
Its day lasts just over 24 hours, a little longer than ours.
The fourth planet from the Sun, known as the Red Planet.
subjects.fact: Its red colour comes from iron oxide, or rust, in its dust.

subjects.name: Jupiter
clues: It has a giant storm, the Great Red Spot, that is wider than Earth.
Its four largest moons were discovered by Galileo in 1610.
It spins faster than any other planet, with a day of about 10 hours.
More than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.
The largest planet in the solar system, fifth from the Sun.
subjects.fact: It is named after the king of the Roman gods.

subjects.name: Saturn
clues: It is so light for its size that it would float in a big enough bath of water.
Its largest moon is wrapped in a thick, hazy atmosphere.
The Cassini spacecraft orbited it for 13 years.
It is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second largest.
The gas giant famous for its bright, beautiful rings.
subjects.fact: Its rings are mostly chunks of ice, some as small as grains and others as big as houses.

subjects.name: Uranus
clues: It was the first planet discovered with a telescope, in 1781.
Its discoverer William Herschel first wanted to name it after King George III.
It is tipped over on its side, so it rolls around the Sun.
It is a pale blue-green ice giant, seventh from the Sun.
The only planet named after a Greek god rather than a Roman one.

links.name: Sun
links.rel: is the seventh planet from the

subjects.fact: Only one spacecraft has ever visited it: Voyager 2, in 1986.

subjects.name: Neptune
clues: It was found in 1846 after mathematics predicted where it should be.
It has the fastest winds in the solar system, over 2,000 km/h.
Its largest moon, Triton, orbits it backwards.
It takes about 165 years to circle the Sun once.
The deep blue ice giant that is the farthest planet from the Sun.

links.name: Sun
links.rel: is the farthest planet from the

subjects.fact: In 2011 it completed its first full orbit since its discovery.

subjects.name: Pluto
clues: It was discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh at an observatory in Arizona.
An 11-year-old girl in England suggested its name.
Its largest moon, Charon, is about half its width.
The New Horizons probe flew past it in 2015 and saw a heart-shaped plain.
Once called the ninth planet, it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

links.name: Eris
links.rel: lost its planet status partly because of

subjects.fact: Some of Clyde Tombaugh's ashes travelled past it aboard New Horizons.

subjects.name: Ceres
clues: It was found on 1 January 1801 by the Italian astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi.
For about half a century it was counted as a planet.
NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited it and studied bright salty spots in a crater.
It is the largest object in the asteroid belt.
The only dwarf planet in the inner solar system, between Mars and Jupiter.
subjects.fact: It is named after the Roman goddess of farming, whose name also gave us the word 'cereal'.

subjects.name: Eris
clues: It was discovered in 2005 by a team led by astronomer Mike Brown.
It is almost exactly as wide as Pluto, but heavier.
Its discovery pushed astronomers to define the word 'planet' in 2006.
It has one known moon, named Dysnomia.
Distant dwarf planet named after the Greek goddess of strife and discord.

links.name: Pluto
links.rel: is almost the same size as

subjects.fact: It takes more than 550 years to orbit the Sun.

subjects.name: Haumea
clues: It was found in the icy region beyond Neptune in the mid-2000s.
It spins about once every four hours, which stretches it into an egg shape.
In 2017 astronomers discovered that it has a ring.
It has two small moons, named Hi'iaka and Namaka.
Dwarf planet named after the Hawaiian goddess of childbirth.

links.name: Pluto
links.rel: is a fellow dwarf planet of

subjects.fact: It is one of the fastest-spinning large objects known in the solar system.

subjects.name: Moon
clues: It always shows the same face to Earth.
It drifts about 3.8 centimetres farther away from Earth every year.
Its gravity is the main cause of the ocean tides.
Twelve astronauts walked on its surface between 1969 and 1972.
Earth's only natural satellite, which goes through phases from new to full.
subjects.fact: With no wind to blow them away, astronauts' footprints there could last for millions of years.

subjects.name: Titan
clues: It is the only moon with a thick atmosphere.
It has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.
The Huygens probe parachuted down to its surface in 2005.
It is bigger than the planet Mercury.
Saturn's largest moon.
subjects.fact: The Huygens landing is still the most distant landing ever made by a spacecraft.

subjects.name: Europa
clues: It was discovered by Galileo in January 1610.
Its icy surface is criss-crossed by long cracks and ridges.
Scientists think a salty ocean lies beneath its frozen crust.
NASA launched the Clipper mission in 2024 to study it.
Icy moon of Jupiter that may have the right conditions for life.
subjects.fact: Its hidden ocean may hold more water than all of Earth's oceans combined.

subjects.name: Io
clues: It was one of four moons discovered by Galileo in 1610.
It is the most volcanically active world in the solar system.
Tidal squeezing by its giant planet heats its interior.
Sulphur paints its surface in yellow, orange and red.
The innermost of Jupiter's four large moons, covered in volcanoes.
subjects.fact: Its volcanic plumes can shoot material hundreds of kilometres above its surface.

subjects.name: Sun
clues: It is a yellow dwarf star about 4.6 billion years old.
Its light takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
It holds more than 99.8 percent of all the mass in the solar system.
Sunspots, solar flares and the solar wind all come from it.
The star at the centre of our solar system.
subjects.fact: About 1.3 million Earths could fit inside it.

subjects.name: Sirius
clues: It is a double star; its faint companion is a white dwarf.
It lies about 8.6 light-years away, one of our closest stellar neighbours.
Ancient Egyptians linked its rising to the yearly flooding of the Nile.
It is the main star of the constellation Canis Major, the Great Dog.
The brightest star in the night sky.

links.name: Sun
links.rel: is about twice as massive as the

subjects.fact: The phrase 'dog days of summer' comes from its seasonal rising.

subjects.name: Polaris
clues: It is actually a system of several stars, not a single star.
It sits at the end of the handle of the Little Dipper.
Two stars of the Big Dipper point straight towards it.
It barely moves in the sky while the other stars circle around it.
The star almost directly above Earth's North Pole, used by travellers to find north.

links.name: Earth
links.rel: sits almost above the North Pole of

subjects.fact: Because Earth's axis slowly wobbles, other stars will take its place as pole star in the far future.

subjects.name: Betelgeuse
clues: Its brightness rises and falls, as John Herschel noted in 1836.
It is a red supergiant, one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye.
If it replaced our Sun, it would stretch beyond the orbit of Mars.
It dimmed strangely in late 2019, stirring talk of a coming supernova.
The bright red star on Orion's shoulder.
subjects.fact: It is expected to explode as a supernova one day, though probably not for about 100,000 years.

subjects.name: Milky Way
clues: It is a barred spiral about 100,000 light-years across.
A supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A* lies at its centre.
It contains somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars.
In about 4.5 billion years it is expected to merge with the Andromeda Galaxy.
Our home galaxy, seen as a pale band of light across dark skies.

links.name: Andromeda Galaxy
links.rel: will one day merge with the

subjects.fact: Its name comes from a Greek myth about milk spilled across the sky by the goddess Hera.

subjects.name: Andromeda Galaxy
clues: The Persian astronomer al-Sufi described it in 964 as a 'small cloud'.
It lies about 2.5 million light-years from us.
It holds roughly a trillion stars.
It is the most distant object most people can see with the naked eye.
The nearest large spiral neighbour of the Milky Way, on course to collide with it.
subjects.fact: It is moving towards us at about 110 kilometres per second.

subjects.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
clues: In 1987 a supernova in it was the closest seen from Earth in almost four centuries.
It contains the Tarantula Nebula, a giant star-forming region.
It is a satellite of our own galaxy, about 160,000 light-years away.
It is easily seen with the naked eye, but only from the Southern Hemisphere.
Small companion galaxy named after the Portuguese explorer whose expedition circled the globe.
subjects.fact: It has a smaller sibling, the Small Magellanic Cloud, also visible in southern skies.

subjects.name: Whirlpool Galaxy
clues: Charles Messier found it in 1773.
In 1845 Lord Rosse sketched its spiral arms, the first time such a shape was seen.
It is interacting with a smaller companion at the tip of one arm.
It lies close to the handle of the Big Dipper.
A grand spiral named for its swirling, water-like shape.
subjects.fact: Though tens of millions of light-years away, it can be spotted with good binoculars.

subjects.name: Halley's Comet
clues: Its return in 1758 was predicted decades ahead, proving it follows an orbit.
It appears on the Bayeux Tapestry, seen in the sky before the Battle of Hastings.
The writer Mark Twain was born and died in years when it appeared.
It can be seen from Earth about every 75 to 76 years.
The famous periodic visitor named after an English astronomer, last seen in 1986.
subjects.fact: It is next expected to return in 2061.

subjects.name: Comet Hale-Bopp
clues: Two men in different US states spotted it on the same night in July 1995.
It was found unusually far from the Sun, beyond the orbit of Jupiter.
It showed both a white dust tail and a blue gas tail.
It stayed visible to the naked eye for about 18 months.
The great bright icy visitor that dazzled skywatchers around the world in 1997.

links.name: Jupiter
links.rel: was found beyond the orbit of

subjects.fact: It will not return for more than 2,000 years.

subjects.name: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9
clues: It was discovered in 1993 by a husband-and-wife team and a fellow skywatcher.
A close pass by a giant planet had torn it into more than 20 pieces.
Its fragments smashed into Jupiter over six days in July 1994.
The impacts left dark scars bigger than Earth in a planet's clouds.
The first collision between two solar system bodies ever directly observed.
subjects.fact: Co-discoverer Eugene Shoemaker later became the only person whose ashes rest on the Moon.

subjects.name: Comet 67P
clues: It was discovered in 1969 on photographs taken by Soviet astronomers.
Its odd two-lobed shape is often compared to a rubber duck.
It circles the Sun about every six and a half years.
The Rosetta spacecraft orbited it for about two years.
The icy body where the Philae lander touched down in 2014, the first landing of its kind.

links.name: European Space Agency
links.rel: was visited by a probe of the

subjects.fact: Philae bounced twice before settling in a shady spot on its surface.

subjects.name: Apollo 11
clues: It was launched on 16 July 1969 from Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
A Saturn V rocket carried its crew of three into space.
Its lunar module was named Eagle and its command module Columbia.
Michael Collins stayed in orbit while his two crewmates walked on the surface.
The 1969 mission in which Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon.
subjects.fact: The crew left a plaque reading 'We came in peace for all mankind'.

subjects.name: Apollo 13
clues: It was launched in April 1970 as the third planned crewed lunar landing.
An oxygen tank exploded about two days after launch.
The crew used the lunar module as a lifeboat to survive.
Its crew were Jim Lovell, Fred Haise and Jack Swigert.
The mission behind the famous words 'Houston, we've had a problem'.
subjects.fact: A 1995 film starring Tom Hanks told the story of the mission.

subjects.name: Vostok 1
clues: Launched on 12 April 1961, it made a single orbit of Earth.
The whole flight lasted about 108 minutes.
Its pilot ejected and came down by parachute, separately from the capsule.
Before liftoff its pilot famously said 'Poyekhali!', meaning 'Let's go!'
The Soviet mission that carried Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space.
subjects.fact: 12 April is now marked by the UN as the International Day of Human Space Flight.

subjects.name: Chandrayaan-3
clues: It was launched in July 2023 from the island of Sriharikota.
Its lander was named Vikram and its rover Pragyan.
It touched down near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023.
It made its country only the fourth to make a soft landing on the Moon.
India's successful Moon landing mission, which followed a failed attempt in 2019.
subjects.fact: Its landing site was named Shiv Shakti Point.

subjects.name: Sputnik 1
clues: It was a polished metal ball about 58 centimetres wide.
Four long antennas trailed behind it.
Radio listeners around the world could hear its simple beeping signal.
It was launched on 4 October 1957 by the Soviet Union.
The first artificial satellite to orbit Earth.
subjects.fact: Its batteries ran out after about three weeks, and it burned up in early 1958.

subjects.name: Voyager 1
clues: It was launched in September 1977, about two weeks after its twin.
It carries a golden record with sounds and pictures of life on Earth.
In 1990 it took the famous 'Pale Blue Dot' photo of Earth.
In 2012 it became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space.
The NASA probe that is the most distant human-made object from Earth.
subjects.fact: Radio signals from it now take nearly a full day to reach Earth.

subjects.name: International Space Station
clues: Its first module was launched in November 1998.
It has had crews living aboard without a break since November 2000.
It circles Earth about every 90 minutes, around 16 times a day.
It was built in orbit by five partner agencies, including NASA and Roscosmos.
The largest crewed laboratory in orbit, about the size of a football field.
subjects.fact: It can often be seen from the ground as a fast-moving bright light.

subjects.name: Space Shuttle
clues: Its first flight, by the orbiter Columbia, lifted off in April 1981.
It took off like a rocket and landed on a runway like a glider.
It carried the Hubble observatory into orbit in 1990.
Five orbiters flew 135 missions over 30 years.
NASA's reusable winged orbiter, retired in 2011.
subjects.fact: Discovery flew the most missions of any orbiter, 39 in total.

subjects.name: Curiosity
clues: It landed in Gale Crater in August 2012.
A rocket-powered 'sky crane' lowered it to the ground on cables.
It is about the size of a small car and runs on nuclear power.
It found that its landing area once held lakes that could have supported tiny life.
NASA's car-sized rover exploring the surface of Mars.
subjects.fact: On the first anniversary of its landing, it played 'Happy Birthday' to itself.

subjects.name: Hubble Space Telescope
clues: Soon after launch, a tiny flaw in its main mirror was found to blur its images.
Astronauts fixed its eyesight on a repair mission in 1993.
It was carried into orbit by the shuttle Discovery in 1990.
Its photo of the 'Pillars of Creation' became one of the most famous ever taken.
Famous orbiting observatory named after the astronomer who showed the universe is expanding.
subjects.fact: It travels around Earth at about 27,000 km/h.

subjects.name: James Webb Space Telescope
clues: It was launched on Christmas Day 2021 on an Ariane 5 rocket.
Its golden mirror is made of 18 hexagonal segments.
A sunshield the size of a tennis court keeps it extremely cold.
It mainly sees infrared light, letting it peer through clouds of dust.
The huge infrared observatory seen as the successor to Hubble.

links.name: European Space Agency
links.rel: was launched with help from the

subjects.fact: It orbits about 1.5 million km from Earth, near a point called L2.

subjects.name: Kepler Space Telescope
clues: It was launched in 2009 to search for planets around other stars.
It stared at one patch of sky in the constellations Cygnus and Lyra.
It spotted planets by watching for tiny dips in starlight.
It found more than 2,600 confirmed planets before retiring in 2018.
NASA's planet-hunting observatory named after a famous German astronomer.
subjects.fact: Its results suggest there are more planets than stars in our galaxy.

subjects.name: Arecibo Telescope
clues: Its huge dish was built into a natural sinkhole in the hills.
For over 50 years it had the largest single radio dish in the world.
In 1974 it beamed a famous radio message towards a distant star cluster.
It appeared in the James Bond film GoldenEye.
The giant radio dish in Puerto Rico that collapsed in 2020.
subjects.fact: Its dish was 305 metres across.

subjects.name: Neil Armstrong
clues: He studied aeronautical engineering at Purdue University.
As a test pilot he flew the X-15 rocket plane.
In 1966 he made the first docking of two spacecraft, on Gemini 8.
He commanded the Apollo 11 mission in July 1969.
The first person to walk on the Moon, who spoke of 'one small step'.

links.name: Moon
links.rel: was the first to walk on the

subjects.fact: He carried a piece of the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer with him to the Moon.

subjects.name: Buzz Aldrin
clues: He earned a doctorate from MIT on how spacecraft can meet up in orbit.
On Gemini 12 in 1966 he showed that astronauts could work well outside a spacecraft.
He was the lunar module pilot of Apollo 11.
In 1988 he legally changed his first name to his childhood nickname.
The second person to walk on the Moon, after Neil Armstrong.
subjects.fact: Toy Story's Buzz Lightyear is widely said to be named after him.

subjects.name: Yuri Gagarin
clues: He trained as a foundry worker before learning to fly.
He was a Soviet Air Force pilot chosen from a large group of candidates.
His capsule, Vostok 1, orbited Earth once in 1961.
After his flight he became a worldwide celebrity and toured many countries.
The Soviet cosmonaut who became the first human in space.
subjects.fact: He was just 27 years old when he made his historic flight.

subjects.name: Valentina Tereshkova
clues: Before becoming a cosmonaut she worked in a textile factory.
Her hobby of skydiving helped her get selected for training.
Her call sign during her flight was 'Chaika', meaning seagull.
In June 1963 she orbited Earth 48 times aboard Vostok 6.
The first woman to fly in space.
subjects.fact: She remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

subjects.name: Sally Ride
clues: She was a nationally ranked junior tennis player before choosing science.
She earned a PhD in physics from Stanford University.
She operated the shuttle's robotic arm in orbit.
In June 1983 she flew aboard the shuttle Challenger.
The first American woman in space.
subjects.fact: At 32, she was also the youngest American to have flown in space at that time.

subjects.name: NASA
clues: It was founded in 1958, months after the launch of Sputnik 1.
Its round blue logo is nicknamed 'the meatball'.
Its Mission Control center is in Houston, Texas.
It ran the Apollo program that put people on the Moon.
The US government agency behind its astronauts, rockets and planet probes.
subjects.fact: Its headquarters are in Washington, D.C.

subjects.name: European Space Agency
clues: It was set up in 1975 and has its headquarters in Paris.
It launches rockets from Kourou in French Guiana, in South America.
Its Rosetta mission landed a probe on a comet in 2014.
It provided the Ariane 5 rocket that launched the Webb observatory.
Organisation through which more than 20 countries of the continent explore the cosmos together.
subjects.fact: Launching from near the equator gives its rockets an extra boost from Earth's spin.

subjects.name: Roscosmos
clues: It was set up in the early 1990s after the Soviet Union broke up.
It carries on the program that launched Sputnik 1 and Yuri Gagarin.
For years its Soyuz rockets were the only way to fly crews to the ISS.
Its main launch site is Baikonur, which it leases from Kazakhstan.
Russia's state space agency, based in Moscow.
subjects.fact: Its Soyuz spacecraft design has carried crews since 1967.

subjects.name: ISRO
clues: It was founded in 1969, with the scientist Vikram Sarabhai as a key figure.
Its first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched in 1975 with Soviet help.
In 2014 its Mangalyaan probe reached Mars orbit on the first attempt.
In 2017 one of its rockets put a record 104 satellites into orbit at once.
The national agency behind the Chandrayaan missions, headquartered in Bengaluru.
subjects.fact: Its Mars mission was widely reported to cost less than the Hollywood film Gravity.
